 1   Q   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY IN THIS

 2       PROCEEDING?

 3   A   The purpose of my testimony is to present NMSU’s adjustments to El Paso

 4       Electric Company’s (“EPE” or “Company”) proposed depreciation

 5       expense. I will provide my assessment of the Company’s depreciation study

 6       and propose adjustments to the Steam Production plant depreciation rates

 7       due to the near-term retirements of four units. I also propose adjustments

 8       to the net salvage rates for three accounts.

 9              My silence in regard to any position taken by EPE in its filings in

10       this proceeding does not indicate my endorsement of that position.



11   Q   PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS AND

12       FINDINGS.

13   A   My conclusions and recommendations are as follows:

14       1. EPE has proposed depreciation rates based on a depreciation study
15          conducted on plant balances as of June 30, 2025. While I support the
16          use of EPE’s depreciation methodology, EPE’s proposed depreciation
17          rates for certain accounts are overstated and burden the Company’s
18          customers with unnecessary and excessive depreciation expense, which
19          inflates the revenue requirement.

20       2. EPE’s proposed depreciation rates would increase the Company’s
21          annual depreciation expense by $35.85 million, or approximately
22          31.4%. These depreciation rates are excessive due to the recovery of
23          the remaining investment in plants that will retire by the end of 2027

 5      Rio Grande Unit 6 in September 2025, Rio Grande Unit 7 in December
 6      2026, Newman Unit 1 in December 2026, and Newman Unit 2 in
 7      December 2027. EPE requests the new base rates to take effect on

10      Because depreciation rates are calculated to collect the unrecovered

 1   II. BOOK DEPRECIATION CONCEPTS

 2   Q       PLEASE EXPLAIN THE PURPOSE OF BOOK DEPRECIATION

 3           ACCOUNTING.

 4   A       Book depreciation is the recognition in a utility’s income statement of the

 5           consumption or use of assets to provide utility service. Book depreciation

 6           is recorded as an expense and is included in the ratemaking formula to

 7           calculate the utility’s overall revenue requirement.

 8                    The basic underlying principle of utility depreciation accounting is

 9           intergenerational equity, where the customers/ratepayers who benefit from

10           the service of assets pay all the costs for those assets during the benefit

11           period, which is over the life of those assets. 1                  The concept of

12           intergenerational equity can be achieved through depreciation by allocating

13           costs to customers in a systematic and rational manner that is consistent with

14           the period of time in which customers receive the service value. 2

15                    Book depreciation provides for the recovery of the original cost of

16           the utility’s assets that are currently providing service. Book depreciation

17           expense is not intended to provide for replacement of the current assets, but

18           provides for capital recovery or return of the current investment. Generally,



             1
               Edison Electric Institute, Introduction to Depreciation for Public Utilities and Other
     Industries at viii (April 2013).
              2

                                                 Page 4

 1       this capital recovery occurs over the average service life of the investment

 2       or assets. As a result, it is critical that appropriate average service lives be

 3       used to develop the depreciation rates so no generation of ratepayers is

 4       disadvantaged.

 5               In addition to capital recovery, depreciation rates also contain a

 6       provision for net salvage. Net salvage is the scrap or reuse value less the

 7       removal cost of the asset being depreciated. Accordingly, a utility will also

 8       recover the net salvage costs over the useful life of the asset.



 9   Q   PLEASE FURTHER EXPLAIN NET SALVAGE.

10   A   As noted, net salvage is the value received from the sale or reuse of retired

11       property (salvage value) less the cost of retiring such property (cost of

12       removal). Net salvage can be either positive or negative. If the salvage

13       value exceeds the cost of removal, the net salvage is positive. If the cost of

14       removal is greater than the salvage value received as a result of retirement,

15       the resulting net salvage is negative.

 1   Q   ARE      THERE           ANY   DEFINITIONS         OF    DEPRECIATION

 2       ACCOUNTING THAT ARE UTILIZED FOR RATEMAKING

 3       PURPOSES?

 4   A   Yes. One of the most quoted definitions of depreciation accounting is the

 5       one contained in the Code of Federal Regulations:

 6               Depreciation, as applied to depreciable gas plant, means the
 7               loss in service value not restored by current maintenance,
 8               incurred in connection with the consumption or prospective
 9               retirement of gas plant in the course of service from causes
10               which are known to be in current operation and against
11               which the utility is not protected by insurance. Among the
12               causes to be given consideration are wear and tear, decay,
13               action of the elements, inadequacy, obsolescence, changes
14               in the art, changes in demand and requirements of public
15               authorities, and, in the case of natural gas companies, the
16               exhaustion of natural resources. 3

17               Effectively, depreciation accounting provides for the recovery of the

18       original cost of an asset, adjusted for net salvage, over its expected useful

19       life.



20   Q   WHY DOES DEPRECIATION DEPEND ON THE USEFUL LIFE OF

21       THE ASSET?

22   A   Generally, capital recovery of an asset occurs over the Average Service Life

23       (“ASL”) of that asset. As a result, it is critical that appropriate average



         18 C.F.R. § 201.12(B).
         3


                                         Page 6

                            NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1       service lives be used to develop the depreciation rates so that no current or

 2       future generation of ratepayers is disadvantaged, or improperly subsidized.

 3       If one generation of ratepayers is charged too much depreciation expense,

 4       then a subsequent generation must pay too little, and vice versa.            A

 5       depreciation rate calculated with the proper average service life promotes

 6       intergenerational equity by ensuring that both current and future ratepayers

 7       are responsible for their appropriate share of the utility property that

 8       provides them with utility service.



 9   Q   HOW DO DEPRECIATION RATES AFFECT A UTILITY’S

10       REVENUE REQUIREMENT?

11   A   Depreciation expense is typically one of the largest single line items in a

12       utility’s overall revenue requirement that is ultimately recovered through

13       tariff rates. When a utility updates its depreciation rates, it is effectively

14       updating the amount of capital that is returned to it each year for investments

15       that have been made to provide utility service. The depreciation rates are

16       calculated in a depreciation study. The resulting depreciation rates are then

17       applied to test year plant balances to determine the depreciation expense

18       component of the utility revenue requirement.




                                         Page 7
                            Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews
                             NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   Q   HOW ARE DEPRECIATION RATES DETERMINED?

 2   A   Depreciation rates are determined in a depreciation study using a

 3       depreciation system. There are three components, each with a number of

 4       variations, used to determine a depreciation system, which is then used to

 5       estimate depreciation rates. The three basic components are: (1) methods,

 6       (2) procedures, and (3) techniques. The choice of a depreciation system can

 7       significantly affect the resulting depreciation rates and, in turn, the revenue

 8       requirement.



 9   Q   PLEASE FURTHER DESCRIBE THE METHODS THAT ARE

10       USED WITHIN A DEPRECIATION SYSTEM.

11   A   There generally are three types of methods of spreading the depreciation

12       expense over the life of property. These are the Straight Line Method,

13       Accelerated Methods, and Deferred Methods. The Straight Line Method is

14       the method most widely used by utility companies for accounting and

15       ratemaking purposes as it is easy to apply and does not create

16       intergenerational inequities because it spreads an equal portion of the plant

17       cost across each accounting period. Accelerated Methods result in higher

18       depreciation rates earlier in an asset’s life, and lower depreciation rates later.

19       Deferred Methods have increasing rates over an asset’s life.



                                          Page 8
                           Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews
                            NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   Q   PLEASE DESCRIBE THE GROUPING PROCEDURES THAT ARE

 2       USED IN A DEPRECIATION SYSTEM.

 3   A   There are four main grouping procedures used in a depreciation system.

 4       They are:    (1) the individual procedure, (2) the Broad Group (more

 5       commonly known as the Average Life Group (“ALG”), (3) the Vintage

 6       Group (“VG”), and (4) the Equal Life Group (“ELG”).

 7              The individual procedure assigns a specific depreciation rate to each

 8       individual asset. That is, each asset has its own depreciation rate based on

 9       its unique characteristics and is not grouped with other similar assets.

10              In the ALG Procedure, all units within a particular account or

11       category are assumed to be part of a single group that exhibits the same life

12       and retirement characteristics.     This is the most commonly utilized

13       procedure.

14              The VG and the ELG Procedures assemble sub-groups based on

15       when assets were installed (VG Procedure) or their expected lives (ELG

16       Procedure). These procedures assume that sub-groups within a particular

17       account or category may exhibit unique life characteristics. As an example

18       of the VG Procedure, it may determine that all poles installed in 1985 have

19       a 50-year life, while all poles installed in year 1995 have a 45-year life. The

20       ELG Procedure may assume that all poles that will attain a life of 50 years



                                         Page 9
                          Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews
                           NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


1        should have one depreciation rate, while poles that only attain life spans of

2        40 years would have a different depreciation rate.       The overall group

 3       depreciation rate would be a composite of the sub-group depreciation rates.



 4   Q   PLEASE FURTHER DESCRIBE THE TECHNIQUES THAT ARE

 5       USED IN A DEPRECIATION SYSTEM.

 6   A   There are two techniques used to calculate depreciation rates: Whole Life

 7       and Remaining Life. The Whole Life Technique spreads the original cost

 8       plus net salvage of the account over the average life of the account. This

 9       technique requires that separate amortizations be made to correct for over-

10       and under-accumulations due to changes in an account’s average service

11       life.

12               The Remaining Life Technique spreads the unrecovered cost plus

13       net salvage over the remaining life of the account. The Remaining Life

14       Technique is the most commonly used technique and it has a self-correcting

15       nature that spreads any over- or under-accumulations over the remaining

16       life.

 1   Q    IN YOUR EXPERIENCE, WHAT DEPRECIATION SYSTEM IS

 2        MOST COMMONLY UTILIZED TO DETERMINE UTILITY

 3        DEPRECIATION RATES FOR RATEMAKING PURPOSES?

 4   A    The most common depreciation system is one that consists of the Straight

 5        Line Method, the ALG Procedure, and the Remaining Life Technique. This

 6        system is commonly used because it offers simplicity, efficiency, and

 7        adaptability for depreciation needs. This combination ensures accurate

 8        depreciation rates for diverse asset types while accommodating changes in

9         useful life and net salvage estimates.

 3   IV. STEAM PRODUCTION UNITS
 4       SCHEDULED FOR NEAR-TERM RETIREMENT


 5   Q   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF THIS SECTION OF YOUR

 6       TESTIMONY?

 7   A   This section addresses EPE's proposed depreciation treatment of four steam

 8       production units that are scheduled to retire at or near the date the proposed

 9       depreciation rates take effect: Rio Grande Units 6 and 7 and Newman Units

10       1 and 2. For these four units, I recommend that the Commission set a 0%

11       depreciation rate.   Instead of future accruals, I have reallocated book

12       depreciation reserve within each location and within each FERC account so

13       that these units are brought to full recovery and their going-forward

14       depreciation rate is set to zero. This adjustment reduces EPE's proposed

15       depreciation expense by approximately $5.3 million based on the June 30,

16       2025 plant balances, and it produces more reasonable depreciation rates for

17       the Company's steam production plant.

 1   Q   WHAT DOES EPE PROPOSE FOR ITS STEAM PRODUCTION

 2       PLANT?

 3   A   EPE proposes to increase the depreciation rate for its steam production plant

 4       from the currently approved 3.51% to 6.15%, which increases the annual

 5       depreciation expense for that function from approximately $26.9 million to

 6       approximately $47.0 million, as shown above in Tables 1 and 2. A principal

 7       driver of this increase is the Company's request to recover the remaining

 8       investment at plants set to retire by December 2027.




 9   Q   WHY ARE THE UPDATED RETIREMENT DATES A CONCERN

10       FOR FOUR OF THESE UNITS?

11   A   The Depreciation Study calculates depreciation accrual rates on plant

12       balances as of June 30, 2025.       The new base rates proposed in this

13       proceeding, however, are not scheduled to take effect until January 1, 2027.

14       Four steam production units show probable retirement dates that fall at or

15       near that effective date. As shown in the Depreciation Study at page III-7,

16       Rio Grande Unit 6 has a probable retirement date of September 2025, Rio

17       Grande Unit 7 and Newman Unit 1 each have a probable retirement date of

18       December 2026, and Newman Unit 2 has a probable retirement date of

19       December 2027. Three of these four units are therefore projected to retire

1        before the proposed rates ever take effect, and the fourth is projected to

2        retire within the first year the rates are in effect.



 3   Q   WHY DOES THIS TIMING MATTER?

 4   A   Depreciation is intended to recover the cost of an asset over the period the

 5       asset provides service to customers, so that the customers served by the asset

 6       pay for its cost and no generation of ratepayers is disadvantaged. Because

7        the Depreciation Study calculates the annual accrual rates for these units

8        based on a short remaining life measured from June 30, 2025, and because

 9       these units retire before or shortly after January 1, 2027, the rates EPE

10       proposes would begin to apply only at the point these units leave service, or

11       after they have already left service.        Setting a positive going-forward

12       depreciation rate for a unit that has retired, or that will retire within the first

13       year the rates are in effect, causes customers to continue paying depreciation

14       expense on a plant that is no longer providing service. For example, the

15       Depreciation Study assigns Rio Grande Unit 7 a depreciation rate of 25.33%

16       in Account 314, based on a remaining life of approximately 1.5 years

17       measured from mid-2025. Applying that rate beginning January 1, 2027,

18       would recover from customers a depreciation expense calculated for a unit

19       that is projected to have retired in December 2026.               This result is

                           Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews
                            NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


1        inconsistent with the purpose of depreciation and unnecessarily inflates the

2        revenue requirement.



 3   Q   PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR PROPOSED ADJUSTMENT.

 4   A   For each of the four units, I reallocated book depreciation reserve within the

 5       same location and within the same FERC account, across steam production

 6       Accounts 311 through 316, so that each unit is brought to full recovery and

 7       its depreciation rate is set to zero. No reserve is moved across a plant

 8       location, and no reserve is moved across a FERC account, so my adjustment

 9       does not shift any cost between plants or between accounts. The reallocated

10       book reserves for each unit are shown in Exhibit BCA-1, which presents my

11       adjustment in the same format as Company witness Spanos's Table JJS-1.

12       This approach recognizes that these units are at or near full recovery and

13       will be retired before or shortly after the proposed rates take effect, and it

14       avoids collecting additional depreciation accruals on units that are leaving

15       service.
